lead: A multivibrator is a two-state circuit built from two cross-coupled transistors or two cross-coupled logic gates. Positive feedback forces each side to oppose the other, so one side is on while the other is off. How the circuit moves between these states defines the three types: astable has no stable state and runs freely, monostable has one stable state and gives one timed pulse, bistable has two stable states and remembers the last input. These circuits make clocks, one-shot delays and latches in timers, counters and power-on reset circuits.
prereq: You need: the BJT as a switch and capacitor charging through a resistor (Unit 2), and positive feedback (Unit 4); the comparator with hysteresis is in Chapter 7.4.

sections.h3: Two cross-coupled sides make two states

blocks.text: Build the circuit from two inverting stages and connect the output of each to the input of the other. Each stage is an NPN transistor with a collector resistor, or a logic inverter. The loop has positive feedback: if one side starts to conduct more, its collector voltage falls, it drives the other side off, and the other collector voltage rises, which drives the first side on harder. The loop settles with Q1 ON and Q2 OFF, or Q1 OFF and Q2 ON. Both are stable.

For BJTs, Q1 ON means its collector is near 0.2 V and Q2 base is pulled low through the coupling resistor, so Q2 is OFF. Q2 collector is near V<sub>CC</sub> and feeds Q1 base through the other resistor, so Q1 stays ON. The second state is the mirror image. A trigger or a capacitor can force a base past about 0.7 V or below 0 V, and the loop then jumps to the other state. The three multivibrators differ only in how many stable states the loop is allowed to keep.
An astable has no stable state. Two capacitors cross-couple the collectors to the opposite bases, so each side can hold the other off only for a limited time.

items: Start with Q1 ON and Q2 OFF. The capacitor at Q2 base is charged with a polarity that holds Q2 base below 0 V, keeping Q2 OFF.

That capacitor charges through R<sub>B2</sub> toward V<sub>CC</sub>. When Q2 base reaches about 0 V, Q2 turns ON, its collector falls, and the step is coupled through the other capacitor to Q1 base, turning Q1 OFF.
Now the capacitor at Q1 base charges through R<sub>B1</sub>. When Q1 base reaches about 0 V, Q1 turns ON and the roles swap again.

blocks.where: T is the full period in seconds; R<sub>B1</sub> and R<sub>B2</sub> are the base resistors in ohms; C<sub>1</sub> and C<sub>2</sub> are the coupling capacitors in farads; 0.69 is ln 2 from the capacitor charging from about −V<sub>CC</sub> to 0 V.

blocks.text: Each half period is 0.69RC. With RB1=RB2=R and C1=C2=C, T=1.38RC and f=1/T≈0.72/(RC). This is the discrete transistor form of the square-wave generator in Chapter 7.4.

sections.h3: Monostable, bistable and the emitter-coupled form

blocks.text: A monostable keeps one stable state. A trigger edge turns the OFF transistor ON and the ON transistor OFF. One coupling capacitor now charges through its base resistor, and when its base reaches about 0 V the loop falls back to the stable state. The output is one pulse of width T=0.69RC, where R is the base resistor and C the coupling capacitor. The trigger must be shorter than T; a long trigger holds the circuit in the quasi-stable state, so the pulse lasts as long as the trigger, not 0.69RC. After the pulse, the capacitor must recharge through R before the next trigger.

A bistable removes the timing capacitors and keeps both cross-couplings direct. It has two stable states and no natural return. A pulse at SET forces Q1 ON, Q2 OFF; a pulse at RESET forces the opposite. The state remains after the input is removed, so the circuit is a one-bit memory or latch. Cross-coupled NOR gates give an active-high SET/RESET latch; cross-coupled NAND gates give active-low inputs. A single-input bistable with different up and down thresholds is a Schmitt trigger, covered in Unit 6.

The emitter-coupled monostable shares one emitter resistor. Its cross-coupling capacitor charges through that resistor and the base resistor, and the pulse width is again close to 0.69RC. It gives a cleaner pulse and better supply rejection. Timer IC versions of all three are in Chapter 7.6.

figure.caption: The top lane is the free-running astable with a 0.65 ms period, the middle lane is a single 0.32 ms monostable pulse, and the bottom lane stays high after SET.

spec.aria: Three timing lanes: a free-running square toggling every 0.325 ms, a single triggered pulse of 0.32 ms, and a level that stays high after a set.

examples.question: A collector-coupled astable multivibrator uses C1 = C2 = 10 nF and R_B1 = R_B2 = 47 kΩ. (a) Find the period and frequency. (b) By switching one base resistor to a trigger input, the same loop is used as a monostable. Find its output pulse width.
steps: Write the astable period: T = 0.69(R_B1C1 + R_B2C2).
Compute each RC product: R_B1C1 = 47 × 10³ Ω × 10 × 10⁻⁹ F = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ s; R_B2C2 is the same.
Sum the two products: 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ s + 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ s = 9.4 × 10⁻⁴ s. Multiply by 0.69: T = 6.486 × 10⁻⁴ s = 0.6486 ms ≈ 0.65 ms.
For the monostable use one RC pair: T_p = 0.69 R_B C = 0.69 × 47 × 10³ Ω × 10 × 10⁻⁹ F = 3.243 × 10⁻⁴ s = 0.3243 ms ≈ 0.32 ms.
examples.answer: The astable period is 0.65 ms, its frequency is 1.54 kHz, and the monostable pulse width is 0.32 ms.
examples.check:
R=47e3
C=10e-9
T=0.69*(R*C+R*C)
f=1/T
Tp=0.69*R*C
print(round(T*1000,2))
print(round(f/1000,2))
print(round(Tp*1000,2))

traps: Using 0.69RC as the full astable period. It is one half period; the full period is 0.69(R_B1C1 + R_B2C2).
Forgetting that a monostable trigger must be shorter than the output pulse. A long trigger holds the quasi-stable state and the pulse is not set by RC alone.
Pairing the wrong resistor and capacitor in an astable. Each half period uses the base resistor and coupling capacitor of the transistor that is OFF.
Treating the bistable as a timed circuit. It has no timing capacitor and does not return by itself; it changes only when SET or RESET is pulsed.
Assuming the astable frequency is exactly independent of supply voltage. The 0.69RC result assumes switching near 0 V and V_CC much larger than the base-emitter drop.

quiz.q: How many stable states does an astable multivibrator have?
quiz.a: None. It has two quasi-stable states and keeps switching between them.

quiz.q: Name the two inputs of a bistable multivibrator.
quiz.a: SET and RESET, also written S and R.

quiz.q: Why does a monostable need a trigger pulse shorter than its output pulse?
quiz.a: The trigger forces the loop out of its stable state. If it lasts longer than 0.69RC, it holds the loop in the quasi-stable state, so the output stays at the triggered level until the trigger is removed; the pulse is then not set by R and C alone.

quiz.q: A symmetric collector-coupled astable has R_B1 = R_B2 = 100 kΩ and C1 = C2 = 1 nF. Find the frequency.
A BJT monostable uses R_B = 22 kΩ and C = 47 nF. Find the pulse width.
A student measures an astable frequency that falls when V_CC is reduced from 12 V to 5 V. Give one reason.
quiz.a: The 0.69RC formula assumes the capacitor charges from about −V_CC to the 0 V threshold and that V_CC is much larger than the base-emitter drop. At 5 V the base-emitter drop, saturation voltage and leakage are a larger fraction of V_CC, so the threshold is reached at a different fraction of the swing and the frequency changes.

quiz.q: How can you tell a bistable from a monostable by applying a short pulse and watching the output after the pulse?
quiz.a: A monostable returns to its stable level after a time set by RC; a bistable stays in the new level after the pulse until the opposite input is pulsed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, the same cross-coupled loop appears as a debounce latch for a mechanical switch, a power-on reset generator, and a dead-time one-shot in a PWM drive. IC monostables such as the 74HC123 and the CD4047 add Schmitt-trigger inputs and better timing; the 555 timer in Chapter 7.6 is the common lab version. In CMOS, cross-coupled inverters are the storage cell of an SRAM bit, and the same positive feedback is analysed as a bistable in digital design. Search for CMOS SR latch, retriggerable monostable and astable multivibrator duty cycle.
